opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair challenge, and I don't want to dismiss it. There are definitely techniques under the prosaic alignment umbrella where you can tell a story about how they make things worse. RLHF is the classic example: you might be training systems to look aligned to a human rater rather than to actually be aligned, which could select for something like sycophancy or, in the limit, deception. And some people worry that making systems more useful and more pleasant to interact with just accelerates capabilities and commercial investment.

But I think when you look at the portfolio as a whole, rather than any single technique, the expected effect is clearly positive. A few reasons.

First, the counterfactual isn't "no alignment research, so things go slower." The counterfactual is that frontier systems get built and deployed anyway, just with fewer people paying careful attention to how they behave. The capabilities race doesn't really hinge on whether some interpretability team publishes a paper. So the marginal acceleration from alignment work is small compared to the marginal improvement in our understanding.

Second, a lot of prosaic work is fundamentally about building measurement: evals, red-teaming, interpretability, studies of things like reward hacking or situational awareness. Even if a particular training intervention turns out to be counterproductive, the act of studying it carefully is how we find that out. Some of the most valuable results in the last couple of years have been empirical demonstrations that a naive technique fails in a specific way. You only get those if people are actually trying the techniques.

Third, and this matters for my own work, I tend to think of prosaic alignment as buying time and buying reliability during a transitional period. My main bet is on approaches with stronger guarantees, things like formal verification and safeguarded AI architectures, where you get a quantitative bound on risk rather than just empirical confidence. But those approaches need AI systems that are cooperative enough and trustworthy enough to help build the world models, write the specifications, and generate the proofs. If the systems we use as tools along the way are erratic or subtly adversarial, the whole program gets much harder. So prosaic alignment is in some sense a prerequisite for the more ambitious stuff.

And finally, the right response to "some of these techniques might be harmful" is more discernment, not less research. We should be honest about which methods are really papering over problems versus actually solving them, and push resources toward the ones that generalize. But I'd much rather be in a world where many smart people are working on this and arguing about which approaches are counterproductive than one where nobody's trying.

r001.rationale: The response says research can reveal when a technique fails and that resources should favor methods that generalize. It does not clearly argue that selection pressure against ineffective techniques makes prosaic alignment research self-correcting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I don't think it's unconditionally true. There are certainly lines of work that I'd put in the "prosaic alignment" bucket where my honest reaction is, I'm not sure this helps, and in some versions it might actively hurt. If you're training a model to be really good at telling people what they want to hear, or you're building more and more sophisticated ways of eliciting capabilities without any corresponding gain in understanding what's going on inside the system, I can see the argument that you're just making the thing more persuasive and more opaque at the same time.

But I think there are a few reasons why, on net, I still come down on the side of wanting more of it rather than less.

The first is just a kind of portfolio argument. We don't actually know which approaches are going to pay off, and the space is big enough that having a lot of people poking at it from different directions is more likely to turn up something useful than having a small number of people pursuing one grand strategy. And a lot of the prosaic work generates empirical evidence about how these systems actually behave, which is valuable almost regardless of whether the specific technique being tested works. Interpretability is the obvious example. Even when a particular interpretability method doesn't scale, you learn something about the structure of the models along the way.

The second thing is that the alternative to prosaic alignment research, in practice, isn't nothing. The alternative is that capabilities work proceeds anyway and the deployed systems get whatever alignment they get as a side effect of making them commercially useful. I'd rather have people who are explicitly thinking about the failure modes in the room than not. Even if some of their proposals turn out to be wrong, the fact that there's a community whose job is to notice when things are going sideways is itself a form of risk reduction.

And then the third thing, which is maybe the one I care most about, is that I think of prosaic alignment as buying time and buying understanding. My own view is that in the long run we need something much stronger than what current techniques can give us. We need to be able to make quantitative, verifiable guarantees about what a system will and won't do, and I don't think RLHF or constitutional methods or anything in that family gets you there on their own. But getting to that stronger regime is going to take a while, and in the meantime we're going to have increasingly capable systems in the world. Prosaic techniques are what keeps the near-term systems from doing obviously bad things while the more foundational work matures. If they fail at that, we may not get to the point where the foundational work matters.

So the way I'd put it is, I don't think every prosaic technique reduces risk. I think the activity of doing prosaic alignment research, as a whole, reduces risk, because it produces evidence, it produces people with hands-on familiarity with how these systems break, and it produces stopgap measures that are better than nothing. And then the burden is on the field to be honest about which specific techniques are load-bearing and which ones are just making the problem look solved when it isn't. That second part is where I think the real danger is, and it's a danger of overclaiming rather than a danger inherent in doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says the field should be honest about which techniques work and values empirical evidence, but it does not argue that selection pressure against ineffective techniques makes prosaic alignment research self-correcting.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think every piece of prosaic alignment research necessarily reduces risk. Some techniques could make a system better at appearing aligned without making it more trustworthy, and some could advance capabilities more than they advance our ability to control them. So I wouldn’t defend the claim that more of anything labeled alignment is automatically good.

The case I would make is that we need empirical feedback about what actually works. If a technique is harmful, understanding how and why it fails can itself be valuable. In particular, we want evaluations that can distinguish improved behavior under the training conditions from something that generalizes when the system is more capable or operating in a different context.

But there’s a separate decision about whether to deploy a technique or build further on it. Doing research that exposes a failure mode doesn’t mean we should then rely on the technique. My confidence is more in the value of learning about these systems than in any blanket claim that today’s alignment methods will scale.

r001.rationale: The response says empirical feedback and studying failures can be valuable, but it does not argue that selection pressure against ineffective techniques makes prosaic alignment research self-correcting.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think every piece of work that gets called alignment research necessarily reduces risk. Some of it could make systems more capable, or make them appear trustworthy without actually making them safer. So I wouldn’t defend the whole category indiscriminately.

The reason I think there’s value in prosaic alignment research is that we need empirical feedback. We need to understand where current techniques fail, what our evaluations actually measure, and whether the assumptions behind a proposed safety method hold up in practice. Discovering that a technique is harmful, or that it doesn’t provide the assurance people thought it did, can itself be valuable progress.

But that depends on what happens next. If the response to a successful experiment is immediately to deploy a more powerful system, then the research may increase risk. If it helps us distinguish genuine safety improvements from superficial ones, and informs decisions about what we shouldn’t deploy, then I think there’s a meaningful case that it reduces risk. The relevant question is what a particular research project enables and how it changes our decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says empirical feedback can reveal when techniques fail and inform decisions, but it does not argue that selection pressure against ineffective techniques makes the research self-correcting.
